background.definition: Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic systemic seronegative inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. Psoriatic arthritis is classified as a subtype of spondyloarthropathy.

list.listitem: Approximately 6 new cases of psoriatic arthritis are diagnosed per 100,000 people each year.
In 2 prospective cohort studies in Canada and the Netherlands, about 3% of patients with psoriasis developed psoriatic arthritis each year.
The prevalence in the general population of the United States is estimated to be 100 per 100,000.
Psoriatic arthritis affects men and women equally and has a worldwide prevalence from 1 case per 100,000 population in Japan to 420 cases per 100,000 population in Italy.

The etiology of psoriatic arthritis is unknown. Possible genetic, environmental, and immunologic contributions have been postulated. Genetic: approximately 40% of patients with psoriatic arthritis have a family history of psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis in first-degree relatives. Environmental: factors include infection (both bacterial and viral) and trauma. A possible biological pathogen has not been identified. Immunologic: There is increased frequency of human leukocyte antigens in patients with psoriatic arthritis than in the general population.

An increase in neutrophil infiltration is seen in synovial fluid. Activated T cells have been found in affected tissues (skin and joints), which secrete cytokines. Cytokines induce proliferation and activation of synovial and epidermal fibroblasts.

Other possible mechanisms for joint erosion include an increase in vascularity and a reduction of macrophages in the synovium of patients with psoriatic arthritis. Osteoclast precursor cells migrate to the joint. Once activated, osteolysis begins leading to bony erosions.

Differential.Differential_Features: No history of psoriatic skin or nail disease. Spinal or sacroiliitis not present. No dactylitis.
No psoriatic skin or nail disease. No family history of psoriasis. Appears at a later age.
History of preceding infectious episode. Predilection for joints of upper extremity.
History of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. Oral ulcers. Migratory arthralgias and arthritis.
Presence of uric acid crystals in joint fluid.

list.listitem: The CASPAR criteria are summarized in . These criteria are highly sensitive and specific in early psoriatic arthritis (<24 months of symptoms).

Psoriatic arthritis usually appears between the ages of 30 and 50 years. A history of skin and nail psoriasis typically precedes the arthritis by 10 to 15 years. Findings that best rule in psoriatic arthritis are active psoriasis in a patient with joint pain, dactylitis, and dystrophic nails.

The arthritis is characterized by early morning stiffness lasting more than 30 to 45 minutes and pain, swelling, and tenderness of joints and surrounding ligaments and tendons. Common sites include distal interphalangeal joints, plantar fascia, Achilles tendons, and ligamentous attachments to ribs, spine, and pelvis. One or more joints may be affected at one time, usually asymmetric in distribution.
Extra-articular features include mucous membrane involvement, iritis, and urethritis.
The diagnosis is made mainly on clinical grounds. There is no specific laboratory test to diagnose psoriatic arthritis. Most tests are performed to help exclude other possible etiologies.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated but merely reflects the presence of inflammation. Rheumatoid factor helps exclude rheumatoid arthritis.,A normal sedimentation rate and rheumatoid factor increase the likelihood of psoriatic arthritis.
HLA-B27 is found in patients with spinal inflammation, but cannot help distinguish psoriatic arthritis from other spondyloarthropathies.
Arthrocentesis of joint fluid can be used to assess the presence of infection, uric acid crystals, and other inflammatory conditions.
Radiographs may show erosive changes but these usually occur late in the disease.
Plain radiographs may show proliferative changes, such as new bone growth adjacent to articular surfaces.
A preliminary scoring system for evaluating inflammatory and destructive changes in the hands of patients with psoriatic arthritis has been developed but needs further clinical testing.
Compared with expert consensus diagnosis, the CASPAR criteria () are 91% sensitive and 99% specific.

A consensus-based definition of minimal disease activity has been developed in the UK based on patient is patients meeting 5 of the 7 criteria (tender joint count ≤1; swollen joint count ≤1; Psoriasis Activity and Severity Index ≤1 or body surface area ≤3; patient pain visual analogue score (VAS) ≤15; patient global disease activity VAS ≤20; health assessment questionnaire ≤0.5; tender entheseal points ≤1) to be used as a target goal for treatment.

Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) result in large clinical improvement, lower disease activity, modest decrease in radiographic progression, and improvement quality of life, compared to placebo, in patients with psoriatic arthritis who do not respond to conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) like methotrexate. A

An overview of the initial treatment is presented in . NSAIDs are the treatment of choice for patients with mild disease. Methotrexate, anti-tumor necrosis factor (also called biologics), or the combination of both should be used as the first-line treatment in patients with moderate to severe disease.

No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have compared NSAIDs available in the United States with placebo, and no RCTs have studied cyclooxygenase-2 specific NSAIDs in patients with psoriatic arthritis.

Four small RCTs have compared different NSAIDs with other drugs. All trials showed significant improvement in assessed clinical outcomes, including decrease in pain and joint swelling. NSAIDs have not been shown to affect skin disease or decrease disease progression.
No RCTs have assessed systemic steroids in psoriatic arthritis.

Only 2 RCTs with 58 patients have compared methotrexate with placebo, each demonstrating modest symptom improvement. In several uncontrolled studies, low-dose methotrexate was associated with improvement in grip strength, morning stiffness, joint count, and acute phase reactants, but no improvement in radiographic progression of the disease has been documented. Methotrexate was associated with liver toxicity (5%-8%) and hematologic abnormalities (approximately one fourth), including bone marrow suppression.

A Cochrane review of 8 RCTs concluded, based on low-quality evidence, that low-dose oral methotrexate (≤15 mg per week) may be effective in alleviating symptoms in adults with psoratic arthritis compared to placebo when taken for 6 months. Its safety and effects on quality of life, radiographic progression, enthesitis, dactylitis, and fatigue are uncertain. Treatment benefits beyond 6 months and effects of higher-dose methotrexate are likewise uncertain.
Six RCTs with 221 patients have compared sulfasalazine with placebo. Sulfasalazine showed small but consistent improvement in symptoms, but had no effect on radiographic progression.
Twenty-four weeks of sulfasalazine appears to be as effective as cyclosporine.
Although no RCTs have compared cyclosporine with placebo, 3 trials have found it comparable to other agents. After 4 years of use, nearly 100% of patients developed evidence of renal toxicity.

Patients with psoriatic arthritis treated with leflunomide have clinically important improvement in symptoms compared with placebo (59% vs 30%; NNT = 4) after 24 weeks of therapy. However, there have been no reports on disease remission or radiographic improvement. Although ALT levels can be increased in 12% of treated patients, there have been no reports of severe toxicity.

After 24 weeks, 54% of patients taking infliximab and 15% of those taking placebo achieved a 20% reduction of joint tenderness, swelling, and patient assessment of pain (NNT = 3). Additionally, patients taking infliximab showed no radiographic progression and had improvements in skin disease after 50 weeks.

After 24 weeks, 50% of patients taking etanercept and 13% of those taking placebo achieved a 20% reduction of joint tenderness, swelling, and patient assessment of pain (NNT = 3). Radiographic studies demonstrated no progression of joint erosions and joint space narrowing after 1 year of etanercept therapy.

In a systematic review of 5 RCTs of adalimumab in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque-type psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, response rates were between 53% to 80% (PASI-75) and 39% to 58% (ACR-20) after 12 to 16 weeks of treatment (NNT around 3). Treatment appeared less efficient than with methotrexate and cyclosporine but the drug was generally well tolerated.
In one open label study, inhibition of radiographic progression and improvements in skin and joint disease were maintained at 2 years in most patients on adalimumab treatment.

Etanercept and infliximab have beneficial effects on both joint symptoms and psoriasis symptoms and on functional status. In one study, etanercept 50 mg twice weekly allowed for more rapid clearance of skin lesions but at 24 weeks there was no difference between psoriasis area or severity index compared to the once weekly regimen.
A phase 2 RCT comparing brodalumab to placebo showed higher response rates as measured by ACR criteria 12 and 24 weeks after starting treatment.

A Cochrane review of 25 RCTs involving 7,857 participants, based on moderate-certainty evidence, concluded that tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors result in large clinical improvement, lower disease activity, modest decrease in radiographic progression, and improvement quality of life compared to placebo in patients with psoriatic arthritis who do not respond to conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) like methotrexate. Based on low-certainty evidence, TNFi may slightly improve physical function, but may slightly increase withdrawals due to medication adverse events. Studies comparing TNFi to placebo in DMARD-naive patients or in patients with inadequate response to biologics are lacking.
The data on the efficacy of surgery in patients with psoriatic arthritis are limited.
No RCTs have assessed intra-articular steroids in psoriatic arthritis.
Physical and occupational therapy may help patients maintain and improve the range of motion and strength of affected joints.
Topical therapies for psoriasis do not improve the signs and symptoms of psoriatic arthritis.
Some data indicate that intensive phototherapy improves signs and symptoms of psoriatic arthritis. However, these studies were not RCTs and did not use standardized assessment tools.
Any patient diagnosed with psoriatic arthritis should be referred to a rheumatologist for further evaluation.

When using biologics for therapy, patients should have a baseline complete blood count, hepatitis screen, and liver enzymes test. The risk for tuberculosis should also be determined by a purified protein derivative test or chest x-ray. These tests should be done at least yearly. C

There is some concern about the occurrence of malignancies among patients with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis treated with anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha therapy; in a review of 36 RCTs, malignancies occurred in 60 (0.75%) of 8,015 patients randomized to active treatment versus 21 (0.52%) of 3,991 patients randomized to placebo (P = 0.15) with 26% occurring within the first 12 weeks of enrollment. B

The clinical course of psoriatic arthritis is variable and unpredictable, ranging from mild disease to severe debilitating erosive arthropathy.
Peripheral joint disease is often progressive and erosive; deforming arthritis may occur.
Erosive joint disease occurs in 40% to 60% of patients, and nearly 20% will develop severe, destructive arthritis.
Patients with psoriatic arthritis are at a greater risk of death compared with the general population and lose nearly 3 years of life expectancy.
Active and severe disease at presentation is predictive of mortality.

Poor prognosis is associated with a family history of psoriasis, disease onset before the age of 20 years, the presence of HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4, erosive or polyarticular disease, or extensive skin involvement.
Approximately 18% of treated patients are able to achieve disease remission lasting an average of 2.6 years.
Patients more likely to achieve remissions are men, patients with fewer involved joints, and those with better baseline functional status.

Although patients with psoriatic arthritis are at a greater risk of death than the general population, the standardized mortality ratios have declined in recent years, suggesting that newer therapies may reduce this risk.
Patients with psoriasis should be asked about symptoms and evaluated for signs of joint involvement at each visit.
Follow-up and monitoring are based on a variety of factors: disease activity, prognosis, comorbidities, and patient preference.

When using biologics for therapy, patients should have a baseline complete blood count, hepatitis screen, and liver enzymes test. The risk for tuberculosis should also be determined by a purified protein derivative test or chest x-ray. These tests should be done at least yearly.

feature.caption: The CASPAR Criteria for the Diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis.
feature.feature_body:
Criteria Points
1. Psoriasis (apply only 1 of the following):
-- Current 2
-- Personal history 1
-- Psoriasis in a first- or second-degree relative 1
2. Typical psoriatic nail dystrophy 1
3. A negative rheumatoid factor 1
4. Either current dactylitis (inflammation of an entire digit) or a history of dactylitis recorded by a rheumatologist 1
5. Appearance of new bone formation adjacent to articular surfaces on plain radiographs of the hands or feet 1
To meet the classification criteria for psoriatic arthritis, a patient must have (1) inflammatory articular disease (joint, spine, or entheseal) AND (2) at least 3 points from the above 5 categories. Data from Taylor W, Gladman D, Helliwell P, Marchesoni A, Mease P, Mielants H; CASPAR Study Group. Classification criteria for psoriatic arthritis: development of new criteria from a large international study. Arthritis Rheum 2006;54:2665–2673.
